0.title: From Death to Life
0.essay:
“Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life” (John 5:24). Jesus describes becoming a Christian in words we would never have dared to use ourselves. Not a fresh start. Not a better version of the old life. A passage from death to life.

A whole journey in one word

That one word, “passed”, holds a whole journey. It begins before we were born, in the purpose of God. It reaches us one ordinary day through the gospel. It turns us round, clears our record, brings us into God’s family, changes us slowly from within, carries us through every failure and every grave, and ends in the presence of Christ, where we will be like him.

Theologians call it the order of salvation. The phrase sounds dry. What it describes is the most wonderful thing that will ever happen to a human being.

Why trace the steps?

Many Christians are content to know that they are saved, and that is no small thing. But it is a little like being pulled from a shipwreck without asking who sent the lifeboat or where it is taking you. Tracing the steps shows that God has been at work at every point, so that all the praise goes to him. It answers questions that trouble real believers: Why did I believe when my brother did not? Am I born again if I cannot remember when? Why am I so slow to change? Will I make it? And it lifts our eyes to the end of the road, where Christ is waiting.

Where this study fits

Several studies look closely at parts of this story: The Doctrines of Grace, Union with Christ, The Grace of God, Justification by Faith Alone, God the Father, Assurance of Salvation, Fighting Sin & Temptation and Perfectionism & Self-Condemnation. This study walks the whole road from end to end, and points to them along the way.

The chapters

The Golden Chain; The Call That Raises the Dead; Born Again; Turning: Faith and Repentance; Justified and Adopted: The Courtroom and the Family; Made Holy; Kept to the End; and Glory.

For reflection

If someone asked you how you became a Christian, what would you say, and how much of your answer would be about what God did? Which part of the road from first call to final glory do you understand least, and which part do you most need to understand today?

1.title: The Golden Chain
1.essay:
In one sentence Paul gathers the whole of salvation into five verbs. God is the subject of every one of them, and between the first and the last not a single person goes missing.

Five links

“For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified” (Romans 8:29–30).

Notice who acts. God foreknew, predestined, called, justified and glorified. In this sentence we do nothing except receive. Notice, too, what never happens. Paul does not say that some of those he called were justified, or that most of the justified were glorified. The people at the beginning of the sentence are the people at the end. The chain does not leak.

“Foreknew” means more than knowing ahead of time what we would do. In the Bible, to “know” someone is often to set your love on them: “You only have I known of all the families of the earth” (Amos 3:2). This commentary holds that God’s foreknowledge here is his loving choice of persons, not his foresight of their faith; The Doctrines of Grace explains election more fully. The chain begins not with our search for God, but with his love for us before we existed.

Written for people in pain

Paul was not drawing a diagram for a classroom. He was writing to suffering people. Only a few verses earlier he speaks of “the sufferings of this present time” (Romans 8:18), and a few verses later he quotes a psalm about believers “regarded as sheep to be slaughtered” (Romans 8:36). The golden chain is the reason he can say, “And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose” (Romans 8:28). It is an anchor for a hospital bed.

And notice what the “good” is. Paul tells us in the next breath: to be “conformed to the image of his Son”. God’s purpose is not that everything will turn out pleasantly, but that everything, even the worst things, will be used to make us like Jesus. And the purpose behind that purpose is the glory of Christ himself, “that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29). The goal of the whole chain is a family that looks like Jesus, with Jesus at its head.

The order of salvation

Later Christians, reading this verse beside many others, spoke of an order of salvation. Its usual Reformed form runs like this: election, effectual calling, regeneration (the new birth), faith and repentance, justification, adoption, sanctification, perseverance and glorification. The Elizabethan Puritan William Perkins wrote a book on these themes in the 1590s called A Golden Chain, and the name has stuck. The units that follow take the links one by one.

A logical order, not a stopwatch

One thing must be said at once, because it saves believers much needless worry. The order is mostly an order of dependence, not a timetable of separate experiences. Several links happen in the same instant. When God gives new birth, the person believes and repents, and at that moment he is justified and adopted. None of these waits for the others. Yet they still have an order, because each rests on the one before it. When you switch on a lamp, the current flows and the bulb shines in the same moment, but the light depends on the current, not the current on the light.

So you will not feel nine stages. One person’s conversion is a sudden morning; another’s is a slow dawn over several years. One weeps; another simply finds that Christ has become precious. The order is the same in every true believer. The experience is as varied as the people God saves. Do not try to force your story into a timetable, or measure your salvation by someone else’s.

Every link fastened to Christ

The links are not separate parcels that God hands over one at a time. Each one is fastened to Christ. We were chosen “in him” (Ephesians 1:4), called “into the fellowship of his Son” (1 Corinthians 1:9), justified because his righteousness is counted ours, adopted as sons and daughters in the Son, made holy as his life is formed in us, kept in his hand and finally glorified with him. Calvin made the point that as long as Christ remains outside us, all that he suffered and did is of no use to us; it is the Spirit who joins us to him. The study Union with Christ works this out. Here we need only see that the order of salvation is not a ladder we climb towards Christ. It is the shape of the life we receive in him.

Why this brings comfort

Three comforts come out of this chain. Your salvation began before you did; it was not your idea, and it did not wait for you to start it. It will not stop until it is finished: the last link is already written in the past tense. And everything in between is held inside God’s purpose. Your sufferings are not interruptions to your salvation. They are among the tools God is using to complete it.

An example

A woman in the middle of chemotherapy had Romans 8 read to her by a friend from church. She said she had always heard verse 28 as a promise that things would turn out nicely, and she knew they might not. Then her friend read on into verses 29 and 30. “So the good is that I will be like Jesus,” she said slowly, “and the end is already written.” She was not less ill. But she was no longer afraid that her illness could break the chain.

No wonder Paul goes straight on: “What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31).

For reflection

Why do you think every verb in Romans 8:29–30 has God as its subject? How does it help to know that the order of salvation is a logical order and not a timetable? What does it mean for your present troubles that the “good” of Romans 8:28 is likeness to Christ? Which of the three comforts do you most need this week?

2.title: The Call That Raises the Dead
2.essay:
Every Sunday, all over the world, the same invitation goes out: come to Christ. Most of those who hear it go home much as they came. A few go home alive. What makes the difference?

The call that goes to everyone

Scripture rings with invitation. “Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat!” (Isaiah 55:1). To the worn out Jesus said, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

This is the outward or general call, and God means it. “As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live; turn back, turn back from your evil ways, for why will you die, O house of Israel?” (Ezekiel 33:11). This commentary holds that the gospel is offered freely and sincerely to everyone who hears it, and that God grieves over those who refuse. A preacher shy of saying “come” to everyone in the room has misunderstood his Bible.

Yet the call is refused every day, and not because it is unclear. “The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him” (1 Corinthians 2:14). The problem is not a lack of information but a lack of life. The refusal is real, and the guilt of it is ours.

One sermon, two hearings

Paul describes one message landing in two ways: “but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:23–24). Same preacher, same words, same Christ. To one listener the cross is an offence or a joke; to the person beside him it is the power of God.

Paul explains the difference with a single word: “called”. He cannot mean “invited”, because everyone in the room had been invited. He means those in whom the invitation did what it said. This is the inward or effectual call: the Spirit speaking the outward word into the heart with power, so that it is not only heard but heeded. The Westminster Shorter Catechism describes it in four movements: the Spirit convinces us of our sin and misery, enlightens our minds in the knowledge of Christ, renews our wills, and so persuades and enables us to embrace Christ, freely offered to us in the gospel. The inward call never bypasses the outward one. God calls people “through our gospel” (2 Thessalonians 2:14).

Two conversions in one chapter

Luke sets two conversions side by side in Acts 16. By a river outside Philippi, a businesswoman named Lydia is listening to Paul, and “The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul” (Acts 16:14). No earthquake, no recorded tears, only attention. Then, at midnight in the same city: an earthquake, a jailer with a sword at his own throat, trembling, a cry of “what must I do to be saved?” (Acts 16:30).

One quiet, one shattering. The same Lord called both. The effectual call has no standard feel. It has a standard result: a person who now listens to Christ, and comes to him.

“Lazarus, come out”

The clearest picture of all is a tomb at Bethany. Lazarus has been dead four days (John 11:39). Then Jesus “cried out with a loud voice, ‘Lazarus, come out.’ The man who had died came out, his hands and feet bound with linen strips, and his face wrapped with a cloth” (John 11:43–44).

Jesus did not ask Lazarus to cooperate; a corpse has nothing to cooperate with. Nor did he drag a dead body out like a puppet. He spoke, and his word gave the life it demanded. Lazarus heard because the voice that called him made him alive to hear it. Then he walked out on his own legs. That is effectual calling. It does not override the person; it raises him. It is the voice of the God “who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist” (Romans 4:17), the same voice that once said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.

Jesus had already explained what Bethany would show: “an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (John 5:25). And notice that he called Lazarus by name. The outward call says “whoever”. The inward call says your name. “He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out” (John 10:3).

Then Jesus told the bystanders, “Unbind him, and let him go” (John 11:44). Only Christ raises the dead, but he gives his people the glad work of helping the newly raised out of their grave clothes.

Where Christians differ

Arminian and Wesleyan Christians agree that grace must come first, because no one can come to God unaided. They hold that God gives enabling grace to all who hear, which each may accept or resist, and believe this protects the sincerity of his love for all and the reality of our response (Acts 7:51; Matthew 23:37).

This commentary’s view: the outward call is resisted every day, but God’s inward call to his chosen people does not fail. The dead need resurrection, not assistance. Jesus says, “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). If the final difference between two hearers lay in their own response, the saved would have something to boast of, but God has arranged salvation “so that no human being might boast in the presence of God” (1 Corinthians 1:29).

An example

A man in his forties went to a carol service every Christmas because his wife asked him to. He could have recited the readings. One year, during the words “The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light” (Isaiah 9:2), something changed. “It was as if someone had switched on the light in a room I had been sitting in for years,” he said afterwards. “It had been my name on the invitation all along.”

For reflection

Why is it important that the outward call is sincere and goes to everyone? What does the raising of Lazarus teach you about how God brings people to life? How should the two calls shape the way you pray for and speak to those who do not yet believe? Can you remember when the gospel first seemed to have your name in it?

3.title: Born Again
3.essay:
Nicodemus came to Jesus at night with a compliment. He went away with a sentence that has unsettled religious people ever since: “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3:3).

A teacher told to start again

Nicodemus was a Pharisee, a member of the ruling council, and in Jesus’ words “the teacher of Israel” (John 3:10). If anyone could have entered the kingdom by improving himself, it was he. Jesus told him he needed a birth.

Think about the picture Jesus chose. Nobody contributes to their own birth. Of all the pictures of a human beginning, Jesus chose the one in which we are entirely on the receiving end. Nicodemus took it literally and was baffled: “How can a man be born when he is old?” (John 3:4). He had understood more than he knew. It is impossible. That was the point.

Water and Spirit

Jesus went on: “unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5). He expected the teacher of Israel to understand, which suggests he was pointing to Scriptures Nicodemus knew. The clearest is Ezekiel 36, where water and Spirit stand together in one great promise: “I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean from all your uncleannesses … And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. And I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes” (Ezekiel 36:25–27).

There are the two halves of the new birth: cleansing from the old, and a new heart from God. The heart is not repaired but replaced. Stone does not feel. Flesh does. A born-again person does not yet have a perfect heart, but he has a living one: it can now be moved by God, wounded by sin and warmed by Christ.

Paul uses the same language: God “saved us … by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5). Roman Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran Christians, and some Anglicans, read this washing as baptism, which they hold conveys new birth. This commentary holds that baptism does not regenerate: it is God’s sign of the Spirit’s cleansing, so closely tied to it that Scripture can speak of the sign in the language of the reality.

The wind

“The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit” (John 3:8). In Greek one word means both wind and spirit. The wind is free: no one can summon or steer it. It is invisible. But it is unmistakable: you hear it in the trees and see the branches bend. So is the new birth. No preacher can produce it on demand, and no one can watch it happen. But you can see its effects in a life.

Born through the word

How does the Spirit give this life? Not, ordinarily, out of nowhere. “Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures” (James 1:18). Peter says the same: “you have been born again, not of perishable seed but of imperishable, through the living and abiding word of God” (1 Peter 1:23), and then tells us what that word is: “this word is the good news that was preached to you” (1 Peter 1:25). The seed of the new life is the gospel, which is why we keep telling it.

Peter adds something that should take our breath away. God “has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1 Peter 1:3). The new life is not a vague spiritual energy. It is the risen life of Jesus himself, shared with us by his Spirit. God “made us alive together with Christ” (Ephesians 2:5). The life that walked out of the garden tomb on the first Easter morning is the life that stirs in every newborn believer. Each time a sinner is born again, Easter happens once more on a small scale.

Life before faith

Which comes first, new birth or faith? This commentary holds that regeneration comes before faith, and that faith is God’s gift. Think of a newborn’s first cry. The cry does not make the baby alive. It is the first sign that the baby is alive. Faith is the first cry of the newborn soul. The two happen in the same instant, and no one is born again who does not believe, but the order runs from life to faith, not from faith to life. John puts it plainly: “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God” (1 John 5:1). The Doctrines of Grace answers the main objections to this in its unit on irresistible grace.

This does not make faith unimportant. It makes faith possible. When you trust Christ, you are not producing the new life; you are showing it.

You need not remember the date

Some believers are troubled because they cannot point to the moment they were born again. But nobody remembers their own birth. You know you are alive because you breathe, eat and grow, not because you remember the delivery room. The question is not “Can you remember when?” but “Are you alive now?” Do you trust Christ? Do you want to please God, and grieve when you do not? Do you love his people? These are the breathing of the new life. Many who grew up in Christian homes cannot remember a time when they did not trust Jesus. That is no weakness in their story, but a particular mercy.

An example

At a baptism a young woman who had grown up in church heard a former addict describe the night Christ found him. Afterwards she told her pastor she had no testimony worth telling. He asked whether she trusted Christ and loved him. She said yes, with tears. “Then your testimony is that God gave you life so early that you never had to know a day without him,” he said. “That is the same miracle, done quietly.”

For reflection

Why do you think Jesus chose the picture of birth rather than improvement or decision? What difference does it make that the new heart is the fulfilment of Ezekiel 36? How does the picture of a newborn’s first cry help you understand faith? If you cannot remember the moment of your new birth, what signs of life can you see now?

4.title: Turning: Faith and Repentance
4.essay:
The first words of Jesus’ preaching in Mark’s Gospel end with two commands: “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel” (Mark 1:15). They are the human side of the new birth, and they last for the rest of our lives.

Two commands, one movement

Paul summed up his ministry in the same two words: “testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 20:21). Repentance and faith are not two stages, as if we first repented for a while and then moved on to believing. They are two sides of one turn. When you turn to face someone, you turn away from what you faced before. The Thessalonians “turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God” (1 Thessalonians 1:9). Turning to God and turning from idols were the same act.

Christians have long called this turning conversion. If regeneration is what God does when he gives life, conversion is what that new life does first. God raises; the raised person turns.

What faith is

The Reformers and their heirs often described faith in three strands. There is knowledge: knowing who Christ is and what he has done. There is agreement: being persuaded that it is true. And there is trust: resting on Christ himself, personally, for salvation. Plenty of people know the facts and agree with them without ever trusting him.

Picture a patient before an operation. He knows the surgeon’s record and agrees that he is skilled. But he trusts him only when he lies down on the table and lets the anaesthetic take him, for from then on he can do nothing for himself. Faith is not an achievement but a surrender into another’s hands. Its strength lies in the one it rests on, which is why weak faith in a strong Saviour saves completely. The study Justification by Faith Alone looks at this more closely.

And faith is a gift: “it has been granted to you that for the sake of Christ you should not only believe in him” (Philippians 1:29). Yet it is truly ours. God does not believe for us; he enables us to believe.

“He came to himself”

Jesus’ best-known picture of repentance is the younger son in the far country, feeding pigs. “But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger!’” (Luke 15:17). Repentance begins as a kind of waking up. Sin is a form of madness, and repentance is the return of sanity: seeing your situation as it really is, and remembering your father’s house.

Then comes the turn: “And he arose and came to his father” (Luke 15:20). Repentance is not only a feeling but a change of direction. The New Testament word means a change of mind that changes the course of a life; the Old Testament’s great word for it is simply “return”. The son did not first clean himself up or wait until he felt sorry enough. He came as he was. The study God the Father dwells on the father running down the road. Here notice the son walking, because every repentance is a walk home, and the Father always gets there first.

True sorrow and false

“For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10). Two men in the passion story show the difference. Judas “changed his mind” and said, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood” (Matthew 27:3–4). His words were true. But his sorrow turned in on itself and took him, alone, to despair. Peter denied his Lord three times, and then “the Lord turned and looked at Peter … And he went out and wept bitterly” (Luke 22:61–62). Peter’s sorrow brought him back to Jesus.

The difference was not the size of the sin or the tears, but where the sorrow led. Worldly grief is sorry about consequences: getting caught, losing face, damaging a reputation. Godly grief is sorry about God: “Against you, you only, have I sinned” (Psalm 51:4). Worldly grief ends in self. Godly grief ends in Christ. And it is “without regret”: no one has ever been sorry that they repented.

If your sorrow over sin has turned into hopelessness, or into thoughts of harming yourself, that is not godly grief, and it is not what God is asking of you. Please speak to someone today: a pastor, a trusted friend, a crisis line or the emergency services. Christ came for exactly such moments.

Repentance, too, is a gift: “to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life” (Acts 11:18). We cannot squeeze it out of ourselves, but we can ask for it.

A whole life of turning

The very first of Martin Luther’s Ninety-five Theses, posted in 1517, said in effect that when our Lord Jesus Christ told us to repent, he meant the whole life of believers to be one of repentance. Repentance is not a fee paid once at the door but the posture of the Christian life. We do not repent to get back into the family; we repent because we are in it: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

The Heidelberg Catechism describes conversion as two things together: the dying of the old self, which is heartfelt sorrow for sin that makes us hate it and flee from it more and more; and the coming to life of the new self, which is heartfelt joy in God through Christ and a delight to live as he wills. Joy is part of repentance. The turning that begins with tears ends at a feast.

An example

A man had been padding his expense claims for years. Each time an audit came round he felt sick and promised God he would stop. He always started again. One Sunday, reading Psalm 51, he saw for the first time that the problem was not the risk of being caught but the God he had been robbing in front of. That week he went to his manager, admitted what he had done and arranged to pay it back. It cost him a promotion. “I have been sorry many times,” he said. “This was the first time I turned round.”

For reflection

Why are repentance and faith best understood as one movement rather than two stages? What is the difference between knowing about Christ, agreeing with the facts, and trusting him? How can you tell godly grief from worldly grief in your own heart? What might it look like this week to live a whole life of repentance, with joy?

5.title: Justified and Adopted: The Courtroom and the Family
5.essay:
In the moment a sinner first trusts Christ, two things are settled in heaven that will never need to be settled again. A verdict is given, and a family name is given.

Two rooms

Scripture uses two different worlds to describe what God does when we believe. One is the courtroom. To justify is to declare a person righteous in the eyes of the law: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn?” (Romans 8:33–34). The other is the family. To adopt is to take someone into the household as a son or daughter: “And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba! Father!’ So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God” (Galatians 4:6–7).

Both are acts, not processes. Each is done once, completely, and never repeated or increased. You will never be more justified than you were the moment you first believed, and you will never be more truly God’s child. That sets them apart from the next link in the chain, sanctification, which grows through the whole of life. Two full studies treat these gifts in depth: Justification by Faith Alone and God the Father. Here we look at how they fit together.

Two different problems

Justification answers the problem of guilt. We stand before a holy Judge, and the charges against us are true. God declares the believing sinner righteous, not because the charges are dropped, but because Christ has answered them: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). His righteousness is counted to us, received by faith alone.

Adoption answers the problem of distance. We were not only lawbreakers but strangers, outside the family, with no right to the name or the inheritance. Paul sets the Spirit of adoption against a “spirit of slavery to fall back into fear” (Romans 8:15), and slaves, however well treated, do not belong. Adoption brings us in.

Why the courtroom comes first

The order matters. A holy Father cannot simply bring an unpardoned rebel into his house as if nothing had happened. That would make the house unholy and the love cheap. So adoption rests on justification. The Father takes into his family those whom the Judge has cleared, and the Judge can clear them because the Son has paid. The Westminster Confession says it in so many words: God gives the grace of adoption to all who are justified.

And God gives both, because either one alone would leave us short. Justified but not adopted, we would be pardoned servants, grateful but at a distance, always wondering whether we had worked enough to keep our place. Adopted but not justified, we would be loved children with an unpaid debt, flinching at every knock on the door. God gives both so that there is neither guilt nor fear. Romans 8 opens with “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1), and a few verses later we are crying, “Abba! Father!” The courtroom and the family room are in the same chapter, and in the same house.

One God in both rooms

Here is the wonder. The Judge in the courtroom and the Father in the family room are the same person. The one against whom we sinned is the one who declares us righteous, and the one who declares us righteous is the one who takes us home. We are not rescued from God by someone else. We are rescued by God, from our sin, for himself.

And between the two rooms stands the same Son. In the courtroom he is our substitute and our “advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1). In the family he is “the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29). Both blessings reach us in him: “for in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith” (Galatians 3:26). The same empty hand of faith receives the verdict and the name.

The Westminster Confession was among the first to give adoption a chapter of its own, and it is one of its warmest. It says that God’s children are “pitied, protected, provided for, and chastened by him as by a father; yet never cast off, but sealed to the day of redemption”.

Living in both rooms

Many Christians live in one room and forget the other. Some live only in the courtroom. They know they are forgiven, but they relate to God as to a magistrate. Their prayers sound like statements to the bench, and they never quite dare to say “Father”. Others live only in the family room. They know God loves them, but they forget what it cost, and grow careless about sin, or else they fear that each failure might make him reconsider. The answer to both is to remember both. You are cleared, so you need not fear the Judge. You are a child, so you may run to the Father. Neither will ever be withdrawn.

An example

A man came to faith in his sixties after a prison sentence. He understood forgiveness quickly; he had stood in a real dock and knew what a verdict meant. What he could not do for months was pray aloud in the church prayer meeting. When at last he did, he began, “Father,” and could not go on. An older member put a hand on his shoulder and waited. Afterwards the man said, “I knew I had been let off. I did not know I had been taken home.”

For reflection

What problem does justification answer, and what problem does adoption answer? Why does it matter that the courtroom comes before the family room? Do you tend to live more in one room than the other, and how does that show in your prayers? What does it mean to you that the Judge and the Father are the same God?

6.title: Made Holy
6.essay:
Most Christians think of holiness as something they are trying to become. The New Testament starts somewhere else: with something God has already made you.

Already holy

Paul lists sins to the church in Corinth: sexual immorality, idolatry, theft, greed, drunkenness, slander. Then he says, “And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11). “Sanctified” is in the past tense. The Corinthians were far from impressive, and Paul spends much of the letter correcting them. Yet he addresses them as “those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints” (1 Corinthians 1:2).

John Murray, the Scottish theologian who taught for many years in Philadelphia, called this definitive sanctification. At conversion something decisive happens: sin’s reign is broken. Romans 6 says it again and again. We “died to sin” (Romans 6:2). We are to present ourselves to God “as those who have been brought from death to life” (Romans 6:13). And then the promise: “For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace” (Romans 6:14). Sin is still present, but it is no longer king. The old self was put off when you came to Christ, and that fact must now be lived out. The study Fighting Sin & Temptation works through Romans 6 in detail.

Becoming what you are

That is where progressive sanctification begins: the lifelong work of becoming in practice what we already are in Christ. Paul describes how it happens: “And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

Notice the method. We become like what we gaze at. People who spend years admiring money grow hard; people who nurse a grievance grow bitter. People who spend years looking at Jesus slowly grow like him, usually without noticing. And notice Paul’s word: “glory”. Sanctification is glory begun. Glorification, the last link in the chain, will be sanctification complete.

The Westminster Confession describes this growth with a lovely balance: the various desires of sin are more and more weakened and put to death, and the saving graces are more and more brought to life and strengthened. It is not only about stopping things but about something growing. And it is concrete. “For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality” (1 Thessalonians 4:3). Holiness shows in bodies, money, words and the way we treat people. It reaches the whole person: “Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, and may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it” (1 Thessalonians 5:23–24).

Grace and effort together

Who does this work, God or us? “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13). The answer is not that God does half and we do half. God does all of it, and so do we, at different levels. We work because he works. Paul says of his own labours, “I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10).

Timothy Keller often pointed out that religion runs on the principle I obey, therefore I am accepted, while the gospel runs the other way: I am accepted, therefore I obey. That is why the order of the chain matters so much. Holiness grows out of the verdict and the welcome. It does not buy them.

Christians differ here. Some Wesleyan and holiness traditions teach a second work of grace, entire sanctification, in which love so fills the heart that deliberate sin is overcome; at their best they refuse a low view of what grace can do. Higher-life teaching urged believers to stop striving and rest in Christ (“let go and let God”); at its best it rightly insists that holiness comes from Christ, not gritted teeth. And many sincere Christians drift into effort with little grace: grim self-improvement with Jesus as an example.

This commentary’s view: sanctification is God’s work in which we actively cooperate. Perfection is never reached in this life (Philippians 3:12), and passivity is never commanded: “Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord” (Hebrews 12:14). We strive, and we lean, at the same time.

The means God uses

God makes his people holy through ordinary means, not secret techniques. Through his word: “Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth” (John 17:17). Through prayer. Through the Lord’s Supper, where Christ feeds his people by his Spirit as they receive him by faith, and through baptism, the sign that we were buried with him and raised to “walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4). Through fellowship: “let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works” (Hebrews 10:24). And through suffering, which no one would choose: our Father “disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness” (Hebrews 12:10).

Slow growth is still growth

Jesus told a parable for impatient Christians. A man scatters seed, “and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how. The earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear” (Mark 4:27–28). You cannot watch an oak grow. You can only notice, years later, that it has. Many believers judge their growth by the last week, and despair. Judge it by the last ten years. Growth can even feel like getting worse, because the closer you come to the light, the more dust you see. The study Perfectionism & Self-Condemnation speaks to those who are crushed by their slowness.

An example

A man known in his church for his sharp tongue was asked by his adult daughter what had happened to him. He did not know what she meant. She said that ten years ago he would have argued with everyone at the table, and now he listened. He had not noticed. He had simply kept reading his Bible, coming to the Lord’s table and confessing when he wounded someone. The blade had become the ear without his seeing it.

For reflection

What difference does it make to know that you have already been sanctified in Christ? Whom or what do you spend most time gazing at, and what is it making you into? How do grace and effort fit together in your own fight for holiness? Looking back over many years rather than one week, where can you see God’s slow work in you?

7.title: Kept to the End
7.essay:
Between the day God calls you and the day he glorifies you lies the rest of your life: years of temptation, doubt, failure and loss. Will the chain hold through all of it?

No missing link

Go back to the golden chain: “those whom he justified he also glorified” (Romans 8:30). Paul does not slip in an extra link, and those who managed to hold on. That is not because holding on does not matter. It is because God guarantees it. This commentary holds that those God has truly saved are kept by his power and will never finally perish. Assurance of Salvation and the unit on perseverance in The Doctrines of Grace treat this fully; here we look at three short passages that show how God keeps his own.

Following, and held

“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:27–28). Notice the two sides. The sheep follow: that is perseverance, and it is something the sheep really do, every day, with their own feet. The shepherd gives and holds: that is preservation, and it is entirely his. The sheep do not keep themselves safe by following. They follow because they are safe, and their following is one of the ways the shepherd keeps them.

And look at what he gives: “eternal life”. If it could end in ten years, it would not have been eternal. Jesus does not give a life that lasts as long as we behave. He gives his own life, which cannot die.

He finishes what he starts

Jesus once told a story about a man who began to build a tower without counting the cost, so that everyone mocked him: “This man began to build and was not able to finish” (Luke 14:30). There will be no such tower in the kingdom of God. Paul writes from prison, “And I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). The good work is God’s, from foundation to roof. He does not leave half-finished houses behind him. When the day of Christ comes, no one will point at a believer and say, “God began this one and could not finish.”

Keep yourselves; he is able to keep you

The letter of Jude is one of the sternest in the Bible. Almost all of it warns against false teachers who had crept into the church, and against the kind of life that ends in ruin. Near the end Jude tells his readers, “keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life” (Jude 21). That is a real command, and it means effort: building up your faith, praying in the Spirit, staying close.

Then, three verses later, Jude turns from the command to the one who stands behind it: “Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy, to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen” (Jude 24–25). We keep ourselves in his love; he keeps us from falling. Our keeping is real, but his is the one that cannot fail.

Look at how the keeping ends. Not with a weary judge admitting us on a technicality, but with a presentation: “blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy.” Picture the day when God, who has carried you through every stumble, sets you blameless in the presence of his glory, and the joy in that moment is not only yours. It is his.

The warnings in Scripture are real, and Jude shows that they and the promises belong together. This commentary holds that the warnings are one of the means God uses to keep his people, and that those who finally fall away shared the outward blessings of the church without ever being born again: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us” (1 John 2:19).

Where Christians differ

Arminian Christians, and many Lutherans, hold that a true believer can finally fall away. They take the warning passages at face value, as addressed to genuine believers, and they fear that a doctrine of certain perseverance will make people careless. Those are serious concerns, honestly held, and every Christian should share their horror at presumption.

This commentary’s view: the chain of Romans 8:30 has no missing link, and the eternal life Christ gives does not end. God’s keeping is no shelter for carelessness. The person who is truly kept will be found following, fighting, repenting and coming back, as Peter did, and the person who uses God’s keeping as an excuse to drift has reason to ask whether he has ever been born again.

An example

A man in his thirties spent most of his twenties away from Christ. He had been raised in the church, made a profession of faith at fifteen, and then spent years in what he later called one long running away. When he came back, an elder asked him how he had held on. “I didn’t,” he said. “I let go of everything. I just found that he hadn’t let go of me.” He was quick to add that he would not wish those years on anyone, and that while he was in them he had no assurance at all. His comfort was not in the drifting. It was in the shepherd who had come after him.

For reflection

How does John 10:27–28 hold together our following and Christ’s keeping? What comfort do you draw from the picture of the unfinished tower, set beside Philippians 1:6? Why might Jude have put his strongest warnings and his greatest doxology in the same short letter? How should the promise of God’s keeping shape the way you treat a friend who has drifted?

8.title: Glory
8.essay:
The golden chain ends with a word in the past tense: “and those whom he justified he also glorified” (Romans 8:30). Paul wrote it to people who were still suffering, still sinning and still going to die. Yet God speaks of their glory as if it had already happened.

As good as done

Why the past tense? Because from where God stands, the future of his people is as certain as their past. Their glory is not a hope he works towards with crossed fingers. It is written into the same sentence as their calling and their justification. If you have been called and justified, the last word about you has already been spoken, and it is “glorified”. So Paul, who knew suffering well, could weigh it and say, “the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us” (Romans 8:18).

What glorification is

Glorification completes everything God began, and it comes in stages. When a believer dies, the soul is made perfect in holiness and goes at once to be with Christ, “which is far better”, as Paul says (Philippians 1:23); the study Death, Dying & Heaven explores this. When Christ returns, the body is raised and transformed: “What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power” (1 Corinthians 15:42–43). And creation itself will share “the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Romans 8:21). This is where the long, slow work of sanctification has been heading all along.

Like his glorious body

“But our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body, by the power that enables him even to subject all things to himself” (Philippians 3:20–21). The pattern for our resurrection bodies is his. Think of the risen Jesus cooking breakfast for his friends on the shore: the same person, recognisable, yet no longer subject to death. He was not a ghost, nor a revived corpse like Lazarus, who would die again. He was the first man of the new creation.

And his body still carried his wounds. “Put your finger here, and see my hands” (John 20:27), he said to Thomas. When John saw him in glory, he saw “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (Revelation 5:6). In the world to come every tear will be wiped away and every scar of sin will be gone from us. But the scars in his hands will remain, the one mark of our sin left in glory, and they will be the reason we are there.

Death swallowed up

Paul ends his great chapter on the resurrection by mocking death: “When the perishable puts on the imperishable, and the mortal puts on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: ‘Death is swallowed up in victory.’ ‘O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?’” (1 Corinthians 15:54–55). Death stings because of sin, and sin has power through the law, but Christ has dealt with both: “thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:57).

Remember the voice at Bethany. The same Jesus said, “an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out” (John 5:28–29). The call that raised one man for a few more years will raise all his people for ever. The first call brought us from spiritual death to life. The last will bring us out of the grave itself.

Seeing him, and being like him

Here is the heart of it. “Beloved, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Now, “beholding the glory of the Lord” dimly, we are being changed slowly, “from one degree of glory to another” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Then we shall see him “face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12), and the sight will finish in an instant what years of glimpses could only begin. We become like what we behold, and we shall behold him as he is.

The psalmist longed for this centuries before: “As for me, I shall behold your face in righteousness; when I awake, I shall be satisfied with your likeness” (Psalm 17:15). When I awake. Every believer’s death is, in the end, a waking up.

And the glory will be his. Paul says Christ will come “to be glorified in his saints, and to be marveled at among all who have believed” (2 Thessalonians 1:10). We will not be admired. He will be marvelled at in us. Glorified believers are not little gods. They are mirrors, at last perfectly clean, held up to the sun.

The end of the road

The journey began with a call: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden” (Matthew 11:28). It ends with another: “Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34). From the foundation of the world. The end of the road reaches back to its beginning, to the love that foreknew us before we were born. Everything in between, the call, the new birth, the turning, the verdict, the welcome, the slow growth and the keeping, was that love bringing us home.

And at home there is a face. “They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads” (Revelation 22:4). The one who called us by name, washed us, stood for us in the courtroom, brought us into the family and carried us when we fell, will be there. We shall see him, and we shall be like him. Jesus prayed for this on the night before he died: “Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory” (John 17:24). At the tomb of Lazarus he had said to his Father, “I knew that you always hear me” (John 11:42). That prayer will be answered, and the dead who were called to life will stand in the light of his face for ever.

An example

A woman with advanced multiple sclerosis kept one verse on a card by her bed: Philippians 3:21. Visitors assumed it was there to cheer her up. “Every morning I read the word ‘transform’,” she said, “and then I read whose body mine will be like. I am not waiting to get my old body back. I am waiting to see him, and to be like him.”

For reflection

Why do you think Paul put “glorified” in the past tense? What does it mean to you that our bodies will be like Christ’s glorious body, and that his wounds will remain? How does 1 John 3:2 connect seeing Christ with becoming like him, now and then? As you look back over the whole road from first call to final glory, where do you most clearly see the love that will not let you go?
